grade.first_issue: The uniqueness argument combines the two inequalities incorrectly. Writing δ=x−y, the valid combination yields δ²+ε(y)²≥2δε(y), i.e. (δ−ε(y))²≥0, not δ²+2ε(y)²≥4δε(y). Thus no restriction forcing ε(y)=0 follows.
grade.summary: The claimed classification is false: every f(t)=t+c with c≥0 is a solution, so f(t)=t+1 is a direct counterexample. Rule A therefore caps the score at 2. The central uniqueness inference is also invalid (Rule E), and repairing the solution requires a substantially new classification argument.
strengths: Correctly squares and rewrites the original inequalities using positivity.
Correctly verifies that f(x)=x is one admissible solution via RMS–AM and AM–GM.

errors.description: The final answer excludes the valid family f(x)=x+c for every c>0.
The two inequalities involving ε(x) are combined invalidly; the correct consequence is only the tautology (x−y−ε(y))²≥0.
Later the proof changes an existential conclusion ('there exists y with f(y)≤y/2') into the unproved universal assumption f(y)≤y/2 for all y.
In the mixed-case argument, it minimizes over all x even though the displayed inequality with ε(x)=0 is available only for x belonging to the zero set of ε.
